title: Genesee Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Genesee wells have a 320 ft median depth, 7 gpm median yield, and estimated finished-well costs of $26,800-$44,000.
h1: What Genesee Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Genesee sits in mountain bedrock, where groundwater conditions can change sharply from one lot to the next. Records within five miles show 4,107 permitted wells, with 2,587 recorded as constructed. Of the wells reporting depth, the median is 320 feet, and the median reported yield is 7.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, and fractured granite and gneiss can produce very different results across short distances. Neighboring well records, local access, septic layout, and the proposed house location all belong in your due diligence.

sections.heading: Genesee well depth follows the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median permitted well depth around Genesee is 320 feet. The middle half runs from 134 to 552 feet, which is a wide spread for a driller estimating a new hole. About 19% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 26% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 32% between 300 and 600 feet, and 23% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well is 4,095 feet, but that is not a normal bid target. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer; 3,949 wells are in that category. Fractured granite is named on 24 permits and fractured crystalline material on 20. In this setting, fractures control where water enters the hole, so nearby depth is helpful evidence but not a promise.

sections.heading: A seven-gallon yield is a workable local benchmark
sections.html:
Among the 1,166 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 3.6 to 10.0 gallons per minute. The largest group, 62%, reports between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 27% reports between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 3% is under 1 gallon per minute and 8% exceeds 15 gallons per minute.

For a buyer, the 3% under 1 gallon per minute deserves attention because storage and household demand become more important. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, and any production documentation. A permitted household well is not automatically a high-production source, and the 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit is a legal ceiling, not a prediction of what the well will make.

sections.heading: Water levels around Genesee show a deeper long-term pattern
sections.html:
The 185 records reporting static water level have a median depth to water of 100 feet, with the middle half from 43 to 180 feet below the surface. That affects pump setting, electrical planning, and the cost of lifting water to the house.

The decade medians move from 26 feet below surface in the 1960s to 45 in the 1970s, 74 in the 1980s, and 150 in the 1990s. Later measurements show 120 feet in the 2010s and 140 feet in the 2020s. The series suggests water levels became generally deeper over the record, although it is not a continuous measurement from one monitoring well. Treat it as regional context, not proof that a specific parcel is losing water.

sections.heading: Permit history shows sustained drilling near Genesee
sections.html:
Permit activity was strongest in the 1990s, with 916 permits issued. The 1970s had 598, the 1980s 560, and the 2000s 523. Activity then declined to 274 permits in the 2010s and 143 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

Most recorded uses are domestic or household, accounting for 85% of permits. Monitoring accounts for 6%, stock for 3%, and irrigation for 1%. The most active drillers in these records are James Drilling Company, Aspen Drilling Company Inc, and Living Water Systems Inc. Their appearance in the records does not mean one is right for your lot; use the permit history to identify experience in nearby ground and request current bids.

sections.heading: What a Genesee well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock described as granite or gneiss, the drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 320 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $20,800 to $32,000.

A finished system adds the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work. The modeled total is about $26,800 to $44,000. These figures are planning ranges, not a fixed quote: difficult access, casing and grout requirements, deeper-than-expected drilling, water treatment, or a replacement pump can change the final scope. Have each bidder separate drilling, casing, grouting, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and testing so you can compare the same work.

sections.heading: Genesee buyers need to check water, ground, and septic risks
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk are the main physical concerns in fractured mountain bedrock. A nearby productive well does not guarantee the same result, and a shallow water level does not guarantee a large supply. Review neighboring permits near the parcel, not just an average for Genesee, and ask whether any well has a documented low yield, poor construction, or failed test.

Environmental due diligence also matters. The mapped area has 93 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 199 historic mine features, and 56 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites are a reason to test and investigate, not proof that a particular property is contaminated. Confirm septic setbacks, reserve area, driveway access, and a suitable building envelope before closing. An augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin, depending on the proposed use and water rights.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Genesee, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Genesee is 320 feet. The middle half runs from 134 to 552 feet, while 23% of wells are deeper than 600 feet. Mountain fractures make individual results unpredictable, so use nearby well records to refine a bid rather than treating the median as a guaranteed depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Genesee?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite or gneiss. At the 320-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $20,800 to $32,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $26,800 to $44,000, before unusual access or added treatment requirements.

faq.q: How much water do Genesee wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.6 and 10.0 gallons per minute. About 3% of reporting wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the specific well's construction and pump-test records because fractured bedrock can vary substantially between neighboring lots.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Genesee, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and test results, not the community median. The mapped area includes 93 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 199 historic mine features, and 56 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well for relevant contaminants, inspect casing and grout, and investigate nearby environmental records before relying on the water.

faq.q: Who drills wells near Genesee, Colorado?
faq.a: The most active drillers in the permit records are James Drilling Company, with 291 records; Aspen Drilling Company Inc, with 209; and Living Water Systems Inc., with 195. Those counts show local permit history, not a recommendation. Request current bids, references, access requirements, construction details, and a clear explanation of what happens if the hole is low-yield or dry.
